title: OSI & TCP/IP models
description: Layers, encapsulation and where each protocol lives.

questions.prompt: Which OSI layer is responsible for routing packets between different networks?
questions.explanation: The Network layer (L3) handles logical addressing and routing between networks. IP and routers live here.

questions.prompt: A Layer 2 switch makes its forwarding decision primarily using which value?
questions.explanation: A switch learns which MAC address sits behind which port and forwards Ethernet frames accordingly. IP addresses are a Layer 3 concern.

questions.prompt: Which TCP/IP layer corresponds to the OSI session, presentation and application layers combined?
questions.explanation: The TCP/IP model has four layers: Link, Internet, Transport and Application. The Application layer covers what OSI splits into layers 5, 6 and 7.

questions.prompt: Which of these are Layer 2 (Data Link) concepts? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: MAC addresses and VLAN tags are Layer 2. IP fragmentation is Layer 3, and TCP ports belong to Layer 4.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the protocol data unit (PDU) for TCP at the Transport layer?
questions.explanation: TCP data is a segment. A UDP unit is a datagram, an IP unit is a packet and an Ethernet unit is a frame.

questions.prompt: When an application sends data, in which order is it encapsulated on the way down the stack?
questions.explanation: Each layer wraps the one above: the Transport layer makes segments, the Network layer wraps them in packets, the Link layer wraps those in frames, and the Physical layer sends bits.

questions.prompt: What does the OSI Presentation layer (Layer 6) conceptually handle?
questions.explanation: The Presentation layer translates data formats, handles character encoding, compression and encryption. In real stacks this work is usually done inside the application or TLS library.

questions.prompt: Why is the TCP/IP model used far more in practice than the seven-layer OSI model?
choices: The Internet's protocols were built around TCP/IP; OSI is mostly a teaching and reference model
TCP/IP has more layers, so it is more precise
questions.explanation: TCP/IP came first as working protocols and the Internet grew on them. OSI is a useful vocabulary (we still say 'Layer 7 load balancer') but few stacks implement it literally.
